body:
I created these notes for use when I facilitate AI safety courses. I'm sharing these notes early because this issue is topical and I suspect it is better to make an imperfect version available early rather than a much more polished version available later.

Please note: some of this content was taken from Additional Course Context . I decided recently that the content on take-off speeds really belonged in the same document as the content on RSI, so I'll be releasing an new version of Additional Course Context at some point (to avoid spamming LW, it'll likely be Substack only ; none of my work is paywalled). Some of the other content was taken from Notes on “We’re in Triage Mode for AI Safety”. Miles' article has been removed from the governance course, so I was looking for a new home for this content. I wanted to include it in a document that was intended to be shared in all the courses I facilitate.

In Take-off Speeds Rules Everything Around Me , Ajeya describes three scenarios:

Whilst there isn’t a strict definition of fast vs. slow takeoff, possibly the most influential definition comes from Paul Christiano . Back in 2018, Paul was arguing that a slow takeoff was more likely, “There will be a complete 4 year interval in which world output doubles, before the first 1 year interval in which world output doubles. (Similarly, we’ll see an 8 year doubling before a 2 year doubling, etc.)“:

- I’ll observe that many people wouldn't call that a "slow" takeoff!

At risk of oversimplifying, Paul argued that we should prima facie expect a slow takeoff because someone will generally figure out how to produce a “slightly worse” version of AI before someone figures out how to build the better version (he claims this is supported by the historical record of technological development overall).

Yudkowsky disagreed (2021), criticising the intuition that “design precursors with 95% of the technology should at least have 10% of the impact. He writes: “An awful lot of my model of deployment lag is adoption lag and regulatory lag and bureaucratic sclerosis across companies and countries” and “My mainline view is that growth stays at 5%/year and then everybody falls over dead in 3 seconds and the world gets transformed into paperclips”

How should we characterise progress up until now?

If Hanson or Christiano or Karnofsky etc etc believed this was what a "slow takeoff" looked like, they failed to convey that to their reassured, cheerful audience.

Tom Davidson responded :

If you thought this was what fast takeoff looked like, you also failed to convey that

For reference, Eliezer previously defined a fast as meaning, “a timescale of weeks or hours rather than years or decades”.

Paul Christiano has shortened his timelines recently. He says he was "broadly right" that "crazy smart AI is preceded by slightly less smart AI, and the gap is a few years rather than a few months", but nonetheless, AI is moving much faster than he predicted ("I've underestimated the pace of progress multiple times before and never seriously overestimated it"). He now predicts 30% chance of a Top-Human-Expert-Dominating-AI within 12 months if we “go full speed ahead”. He writes:

And even if we ignored the possibility of accelerating progress on deep learning, we'll soon be in the regime where if there was a much cleverer way to build AI systems that humans haven't thought of (which honestly seems more likely to not) then an AI working for a week is more likely to find it than the last 60 years of human progress.

“Bumpy” intelligence explosions

Forethought defines an additional scenario . For example, imagine if AI dramatically accelerates algorithm progress for a while, but then this plateaus whilst we figure out how to make robots that can automate the construction of chip fabs.

(Modified version of Forethought diagram.)

In contrast, Arvind Narayanan (of AI as a Normal Technology ) argues any RSI we do achieve will be narrow (that is jagged): ie. progress on verifiable tasks will continue “for a few more years” or even accelerate whilst progress on unverifiable tasks more or less remains “frustratingly hard”. Elsewhere they’ve framed this as jaggedness applying not just to capabilities, but also to rate of change.

“How did you go bankrupt?”

Two ways. Gradually, then suddenly.”

― Ernest Hemingway, The Sun Also Rises

“Gradually, then suddenly” feels like an underrated possibility to me.

Argument in favour: perhaps there’s a phase transition when human researchers are no longer bottlenecking AI development.

Argument against: improvements in AI-assistance might be continuous and required simply to maintain the trendline in light of decreasing marginal returns.

Whilst this is arguably less relevant these days, take-off speeds is distinct from timelines. Take-off speeds are about how fast an intelligence explosion occurs if/when it happens whilst timelines are about when a particular milestone is achieved. Both slow-takeoff/short-timelines and fast-takeoff/long-timelines are conceptually possible.

Complicating matters further, if someone talks about short-timelines to AGI, it matters hugely whether they mean human-level intelligence (like some researchers have argued that we have already achieved ) or whether they mean a system that is strongly capable of autonomously learning and improving itself. As Ajeya notes , someone might have short-timelines to AGI and then a slow-take off from there, or they might believe that things will move very fast once we’ve achieved the AGI milestone. A fast take-off post-AGI is much more likely if we mean the latter definition.

Of course, whether a “take-off” is fast or slow may depend on when we start counting from. Do we start counting from ChatGPT/GPT4 or only when we hit a particular AGI milestone?

The previous section focused primarily on what RSI might look like in terms of outputs , this section focuses on what kind of feedback loop might be driving this.

Types of “Intelligence Explosion”:

Forethought examines three kinds of feedback loops :

Building on top of this, Forethought defines three kinds of intelligence explosion:

- software only recursive self-improvement

- AI-technology: driven by improvements in software and chip design,

- full-stack where AI also helps increase the production of chips.

The reason why each type of intelligence explosion includes the previous factors is that they’ve ordered the factors by expected lead-time. If an intelligence explosion is possible, fast takeoff vs. slow takeoff likely depends heavily on what kinds of intelligence explosion would be sufficiently powerful to trigger it. For example, a fast takeoff is much more likely where a software-only explosion is possible, however, if you need to automate the full-stack, then there’d be a much stronger argument for a slow takeoff.

We already saw their model of how these different feedback loops could combine depending on the strength of each. I imagine they would have moved a reasonable amount of their probability mass from the “gradual” world to either “rapid” or “bumpy”.

They observe that the feedback loops could be divided further:

Indeed, the AI Futures model focuses on the possibility of a software intelligence explosion and distinguishes automating coding from automating research.

They define the following milestones (see the diagram above for estimated speed-up) where the operationalisations all imagine that we “drop” the AI into the present day:

- An AC can fully automate an AGI project’s coding work, replacing the project’s entire coding staff

- Operationalisation: as productive on their own as only human coders with no AIs (max resource utilisation: 5% of compute).

- Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR):

- A SAR can fully automate AI R&D, making all human researchers obsolete.

- Operationalisation: as good at research taste as if there were only human researchers, who were each made as skilled as the top researcher (max resource utilisation: 1% of compute).

- Top-human-Expert-Dominating AI (TED-AI):

- A TED-AI is at least as good as top human experts at virtually all cognitive tasks.

- Operationalisation: if given the resources of a large tech company & three months to prep, fully automate 95% of remote work jobs in the US.

- Artificial Superintelligence (ASI).

- The gap between an ASI and the best humans is 2x greater than the gap between the best humans and the median professional, at virtually all cognitive tasks.

- Operationalisation: if given the resources of a large tech company & three months to prep, be able to fully automate 95% of remote work jobs in the US to the level where it is qualitatively 2x as much above the best human as the best human is above the median professional.”

AI as a normal technology argues that the slowness of diffusion cycles will provide a bottleneck. Specifically, in their model, it takes time for model capabilities to flow through to product changes and then for people to use them. This produces the data that we need for the next round of capabilities improvements and the dependency on data from deployment limits the speed of potential feedback loops:

## Projecting Trends into the Future

Tim Urban argues that, “it’s most intuitive for us to think linearly , when we should be thinking exponentially ”

This forms a key crux: Can we project exponential trends into the future on the basis of induction (ie. the future being like the past) or is this foolish given that exponentials must end at some point? Development of most technologies has occurred as a series of s-curves (ie. sigmoids) which would support the latter view.

In some cases, a series of s-curves can stack into an exponential (at least for a while). A particularly pertinent example: LLM’s were gaining dramatic new ability by scaling pre-training. When this trend broke, there was a brief period when many people felt that AI was “hitting a wall”, but it took barely any time for two new scaling laws (one on post-training, one on inference) to appear. So when forecasting future capabilities, it is important to not only think about the ability of the current trend to continue, but whether the labs are likely to have access to other plausible paradigms that can prevent progress from plateauing.

On this point, Astralcodex points out that simply knowing that something is a sigmoid doesn’t tell you where you are on the curve (a hilarious graph from the World Energy Organisation shows them repeatedly, incorrectly predicting that exponential progress in terms of solar power will finish):

He also also a graph showing where researchers incorrectly predicted that the METR time horizons would cap out just as the curve zoomed upward):

Connor Leahry writes : “There are only two times to react to an exponential: Too early, or too late.” In many case this is true. However, early on it may be hard to know if it is an exponential or not. Unfortunately, in many cases we’ll just have to make such decisions under uncertainty.

## Are we experiencing RSI?

- A lot of the current discussion of RSI was trigged by METR’s independent report on the automation of research at Anthropic: “We believe that, as of Oct 2026, the pace of capability growth on well-specified tasks is likely about 2x what it was from Mar 2024 to Oct 2025. We’re highly uncertain and would not be surprised by 1.3x–3x.”.

- METR reports that their analysis significantly depends on analysis and evidence that Anthropic didn’t allow them to publish. However Karthik Tadepalli reports on their attempts to verify the report using public information: “The last two steps take the acceleration from 1.64x to 1.9x, METR’s headline, but the majority of the work is in the first two steps, which can be reproduced from public data” (TLDR: Karthik argues that the acceleration is real, AI is likely the cause, but its less clear how far we should expect this trend to continue)

- After publication, Anthropic updated its S-1 form (for its IPO) to indicate that their Responsible Scaling Policy now applies because they “observe or expect” a doubling of their research progress:

Before considering the evidence, it may make sense to examine this crux diagram from the Forecasting Research Institute .

- Skeptical take — My Top Recommendation: Iron Makes Iron by Dean Ball

- Dean Ball distinguishes between weak recursion and strong recursion:

- Weak recursion: “when a technology is a key input into the production of more and better versions of that same technology”. He describes this as, “the historical norm rather than an aberration“, describing ironsmiths using iron to make more iron and railways to transport the material needed to make more railways. He writes: ”weak recursion is not really weak: it is one of the most powerful dynamics in human history, rhyming if not synonymous with the concept of compounding growth. In the context of AI, weak recursion could result in a rapid increase in frontier AI capabilities—more rapid than anything we have seen so far—over the coming year or so.“

- Strong recursion: “when a technology can autonomously plan and execute the development of its successor”. He suggests it is never happened in history; even human brains haven’t yet achieved this. He writes: “strong recursion is a genuine risk, possibly in the near term, though the evidence for it is thinner than is sometimes supposed”.

- He argues that progress on weak recursion doesn’t automatically imply we’ve almost solve challenge of long-range research taste remains particularly ellusive:

- “Some of this work requires taste and discernment—incredibly challenging to measure objectively—and the ability to sharpen those skills over years. Many of the most senior scientists in the field of deep learning, which undergirds all of modern AI, got into the field years or decades before it bore fruit. An empirical evaluation of their research taste would have shown these scientists to have quite poor taste, and quite low research productivity—right up until the deep learning revolution began in 2012. Some AI training environments involve models working for days or more today, but years? It is unclear how we would even design evaluations for long-range intellectual taste.”

- He acknowledges that there are ways for weak recursion to lead to strong recursion:

- Maybe “this characteristic we find so ineffable and mysterious will simply fall out of another round of scaling”

- Perhaps, “the capabilities acceleration that comes from weak recursion will yield models capable of strong recursion”

- Or maybe, “experimentation done at massive scale may be able to serve as a stand-in for taste” or at least ‘blur the boundaries“

- Even so, he asserts that none of these pathways obviously take us from weak recursion to strong recursion.

- Affirmative take — My top recommendation: Recursive self-improvement has started by Dwarkesh Patel ( text version ):

- Last year, Dwarkesh argued that AGI wasn’t “right around the corner” due to AI having poor sample efficiency and a very limited ability to continually learn. Specifically, he predicted that it would take on average until 2032 for AI to be as good at learning on the job as a a human video editor he might hire.

- Dwarkesh is now arguing that it’ll only take “a couple of years… possibly only a couple of months” to reach AIs that are as good as top human AI researchers (he only places a 25% chance on this happening after 2032). Dwarkesh then argues that it would only take a year after that to produce an AI that would be as good as “the best human experts in every field”.

- Dwarkesh starts by arguing that automated AI research is extremely tractable. He observes that recent AI progress has almost all been accomplished by empirical iteration, rather than any kind of deep theory. He then points out that, if we believe Chris Olah, “ the transformer architecture was a natural combination of many ideas”, and you just needed to discover a few tweaks and combine them in the same way.

- Dwarkesh argues that automating AI research will allow us to produce a really strong meta-learner ("The AIs will learn to make their way in an unfathomable number of virtual worlds that are each to today’s video games what a Bugatti is to a horse and buggy. These games will be far more difficult, messy, sprawling, and realistic than anything ever made for human entertainment. They will require AIs to cooperate or compete with teams of other AIs over long periods of time. For example, an AI will be dropped into a thriving simulated digital economy full of millions of other AIs and told to cofound a successful company.” and “The AIs will also train themselves on endless backtests of everything in the history of science and tech and politics and culture—they’ll have to predict every discovery, invention, war, election, and quarterly earnings report that has ever happened.”)

- He argues that we should expect transfer to non-verifiable domains because a) humans managed this b) we’ve already seen AI demonstrate significant generalisation.

- What about his earlier continual learning objection? a) we may be able to extend context windows to several months and this may be sufficient for model to “learn on the job” b) we may be able to crack online learning by pointing automated AI researchers at the right verifiable proxies.

- Jack Clarke has commented that it’s, “more likely (than not that) we’ll see full RSI become possible in 2027”

- Research acceleration: The view inside OpenAI contains a lot of interesting details on where we are with RSI.

- I found the Anthropic self-improvement report less useful, though, like the OpenAI report it also showed their engineers shipping about 8 times as much code.

- Limitations: This is a lot, but it’s hard to know how to correlate it with things that matter given how crude lines of code is as a measure. Engineers estimated the true output increase at 4 times. Of course, we might wonder how accurate subjective estimates actually are .

- More on the METR report:

- Ryan Greenblatt estimates (based on his previous public comments to avoid any risk of revealing confidential info) an AI software R&D speed-up of 3.8x. The reason why this only results in a 2x speed-up in benchmark progress is because a) some increases in the scores comes from scaling compute (he estimates 2/3 of the progress comes from software improvements) b) there are decreasing marginal returns (see below; source ; METR further estimates that the uplift in rate of progress is only 1.7x if we limit it to that attributable to AI).

- Personally, progress has felt a lot faster in the last year. Honestly, I’m still kind of confused why a potential 2x speed increase seems to have been a big update for many people.

- Here’s the self-reported speedups. There’s likely significant selection effects here: employees might worry that they’d look bad if they reported less speed-up than others.

- A P-Zero Research study into AI’s research taste found; “the experimental research taste of frontier models has doubled every ~3 months since December 2025. The best model, Opus 5.5, now exceeds our expert human baseline”.

- Key limitations: “Our results may overstate how fast research taste is improving. Our tasks are fast and cheap to verify, which frontier labs find easiest to hill-climb, and our human baseline doesn’t include top researchers, so it may significantly underestimate the performance of the best researchers in the world. TasteVal also doesn’t measure a model’s ability to choose which problems are most fruitful to work on.”

- Apparently Sergey Brin is pushing Google to work towards recursive self-improvement to catch up to the frontier. The benchmarks for Gemini 4 Carbon suggest that this strategy may have been effective .

Next we’ll consider a tables from DeepMind’s AGI to ASI which lays out potential bottlenecks for continued progress:

Toby Ord has previously argued that many people have failed to realise the implications of the shift from pre-training scaling to RL and inference-time scaling. A 100x increase in pre-training is equivalent to a 1,000x increase in inference or a 1,000,000x scale up of RL . He suggests that this effect has been masked since these factors hadn’t been scaled, but he suggests this is set to change with models already utilising significant inference-time compute and RL assigned a significant proportion of training compute (he has a whole series on AI scaling ).

Is scaling an issue in practise? On the pro side, both Ramez Naam and Seb Krier note that a linear increase in AECI requires an exponential increase in spending.

On the con side, Tom Davidson points out that this might be viable because linear increases in ECI provide (in his view) exponential increases in productivity. Thus the outputs scales with inputs in such a way that it might be viable.

More recently, Toby observes that METR wasn’t confidently able to rule out a one-time jump (say from Mythos having been developed on top of a larger pre-train, which his results suggests scales better) rather than an increase in slope. He performed a quick analysis using Opus which suggested that 1.4x is a better estimate of the new slope gradient than METR’s 1.9x:

In contrast, Jacob Coxon comments on a slide from Anthropic’s IPO roadshow:

It shows the compute efficiency of pretraining over time. The y-axis is a **log scale**: they are seeing continued superexponential algorithmic progress. Mythos was not a one-time deviation, but a point on a superexponential. They could already retrain Mythos with a fraction of the compute originally needed.

It doesn’t strictly imply a software-only intelligence explosion- they have been spending more on R+D. But algorithmic improvements do not require ridiculous creative genius and are on the verge of being automated. You do the math.

Ramez Naam’s Where’s the “Intelligence Explosion”? provides us with some evidence in favour of Dean Ball's perspective. He argues that the current AI feedback loop is only 10-20% of the strength required. He interprets OpenAI internal automation data as showing the real world AI research is much harder than other benchmarks show. This provides some evidence that the issue of taste that Dean highlighted might be the bottleneck, though as Dean pointed out, this doesn’t show that this bottleneck will remain intractable.

This was published 27th Sep 2026, ie. before METR’s independent report on AI acceleration. It’ll be interesting to see his response :

Well, this report finding acceleration of AI progress inside of Anthropic certainly has my attention! Digging in now before commenting much publicly. Thanks all who pointed me to it.

In his original post, he wrote that Anthropic predicted a 40× speed up in researcher productivity would be required to double their rate of progress due to other bottlenecks. It’s interesting that Anthropic claims to have almost achieved this with an average self-reported uplift of only 12x. I wonder what explains this discrepency.

Even though he hasn’t published a complete update yet, he has commented on what the recent acceleration at Anthropic might mean:

Anthropic made faster gains this year than in its past or than its competitors. This hasn't yet accelerated the overall AI frontier pace (Chris: because Anthropic was behind). If Anthropic keeps up this pace, the overall AI frontier will accelerate. If these were catch-up gains, it may not.

We previously saw that Arvind Narayanan expects any RSI to be narrow. Richard Ngo agrees that we should expect jaggedness to persist, as opposed to everything “going vertical”. Why? Because of a poorly understood “divergence” between “measured capabilities” and “real-world impacts”. Nonetheless, unlike Arvind he asserts “things are going to look much weirder than almost anyone expects.

In contrast, Paul Christiano argues that progress won’t be limited to verifiable tasks because a) strong performance on a sufficiently wide range of verifiable virtual tasks requires developing a superhuman learner (which can then be trained on real-world data), rather than just memorising the distribution b) he suspects that current spillover, plus a rapid acceleration would lead to broad superintelligence c) AI can dramatically accelerate the process of adapting AI to be usable in the real world.

## If it does happen, how might it play out?

We’ll begin by naively projecting the METR results forward:

Ajeya Cotra writes : If we take it at face value that AI is now nearly doubling the rate of AI capabilities progress and assume acceleration from AI is smooth, this naively implies that we would reach extreme superintelligence within a year

Benjamin Todd comments on this:

The dumbest possible way to model the intelligence explosion says you get there in about a year. But this seems to line up with more sophisticated models (like from the AI Futures Project).

So what might it look like if this model turn out to be accurate, or at least, “accurate enough”? Tim Urban argues that we have a distorted view of intelligence because are perceptions are very human centric (and, as such, stretch out the human range):

Conversely Steve Newman offers the following frame : what if AI is moving fast, but the “distance” to travel is longer than most people think, since we often only become aware of the limitations of models over time?:

- “The real challenges may be things that we can’t easily anticipate right now, weaknesses that we will only start to put our finger on when we observe Claude 5 or o3 performing astonishing feats and yet somehow still not being able to write that tightly-plotted novel.”

- “People usually frame AI progress in terms of a single variable: the rate of progress. They think of AI as either a speedboat, rapidly crossing a lake; or something more like a rowboat, whose tired occupant, after an initial burst of speed, still has a long journey ahead. I think a better analogy would be a speedboat crossing the Pacific Ocean. Current AIs are both astoundingly useful, and limited in many ways. The ocean we call “intelligence” is wider than we can easily appreciate, and will take a long time to cross.”

(Of course, it is possible that both could be true at the same time)

Samuel Hammond takes a very aggressive view of what RSI would mean:

In the pre-RSI regime, human frictions created automatic buffers between new model releases, giving researchers and society time to probe emergent capabilities, design better evals, develop novel alignment techniques, and adapt / harden their infrastructure. As progress has accelerated, capability improvements have already started outstripping our adaptive capacity, as manifest in METR's inability to evaluate model autonomy beyond 13 hours, and narrow window for cyber defenders to prepare for open weight versions of Mythos.

RSI will exacerbate all these issues and create all new ones.

At minimum, we should anticipate:

- the equivalent of a GPT-5.2 -> 5.6 leap in capabilities at least every 24 hours (down from 3-6 months),

- concurrent algorithmic improvements densifying models to ultra-efficient sizes at any given capability level

- 100x Mythos-like capabilities across most verifiable domains, including chem, nuclear and bio

- new forms of multi-agent misalignment risk

- "company in a box" agents trained to stand-up whole organizations / corporations

- "cyber nuke"-like capabilities that require de minimis infra

- several transformer-scale breakthroughs, such as for long-term memory / continual learning, open-ended domains, and/or all-new training techniques for idealized "GPT-zero"-esque metalearners

- concurrent speedups in any complementary technical domain, i.e. explosive rates of R&D and novel discoveries

Note that Samuel claims: “The equivalent of a GPT-5.2 → 5.6 leap in capabilities at least every 24 hours (down from 3-6 months)“. Why? His answer :

If you do a simple linear regression on model release cadence it predicts a new frontier model will be produced roughly every day by January 2027. Whether a daily release cadence makes any sense is another question. By that point I suspect new models will be private by default.

The question I want him to answer is: “Wouldn’t the training runs take a certain amount of time even if the research itself is automated?”

Dwarkesh provides Samuel with a possible answer :

Because smaller models train faster, this tightens the RSI loop itself. During RSI, labs probably won’t do three-month pretraining runs spread across multiple datacenter campuses. The army of automated researchers would be finding algorithmic innovations so quickly that, by the time a giant run finished, it would already be made obsolete by a much smaller model that first began training only a week ago. It’s similar to how, if you launched a spaceship to Alpha Centauri with today’s technology, it would probably be overtaken in transit by one launched a century from now. Furthermore, since you’re training smaller models faster, on a scale where you can run thousands of experiments daily, you won’t have to bet that small-scale results will hold up in bigger models. You’ve already tested at the scale you’re training.
